source: Thompson, Prowse Turner and Pennycook (2011) Intuition, reason, and metacognition. Cognitive Psychology 63(3)
finding: Four experiments with a two-response paradigm. Low feeling of rightness (FOR) on the first answer went with longer rethinking time and a higher chance of changing the answer. FOR was predicted by how fluently the first answer came to mind.
numbers: Sample sizes: conditional reasoning N=60; three-term conditional reasoning N=48; base-rate problems N=128; syllogisms N=64 (total 300). The abstract gives no effect sizes.
limits: Abstract only (via Europe PMC); the full paper was behind a 403 wall, so exact correlations and coefficients are still unseen. Thompson and Johnson 2014 could not be retrieved at all.
agent_relevance: Founding evidence for G1: the trigger is a cheap judgment on the first answer, and its strength sets how much extra thinking follows.

source: Thompson and Markovits (2025) Fast reasoning and metacognition. Psychonomic Bulletin and Review
finding: Extends the FOR finding. Low FOR on a belief-based answer led to a shift toward logic-based answers when time was unconstrained; high FOR led to a shift toward belief. FOR predicts the direction of change, not only the amount.
numbers: N=289, two blocks of belief-logic conflict syllogisms (first under time limit, second unconstrained). The abstract restates the 2011 link between FOR, thinking time and answer change as established.
limits: Abstract only. Same research tradition as the founder (Thompson), so not an independent lab. Syllogisms only.
agent_relevance: Rethinking after a low-certainty first pass can move the answer either way; a trigger should not assume the second answer is better.

source: Response generation, not response execution, influences feelings of rightness in reasoning (2023) Q J Exp Psychol
finding: Two experiments tested whether FOR depends on how fast the answer is output or how fast it is generated. Output duration had no effect on FOR or reflection. Answer fluency in generation is the driver, as the original theory says.
numbers: Two experiments; the abstract gives no sample size or effect size. Data on OSF.
limits: Abstract only. It supports the fluency account, but it is a manipulation test, not a direct replication of the FOR to rethink-time link.
agent_relevance: For an LLM, the nearest analogue of fluency is sampling agreement or token probability of the first answer, not output length.

source: Conflict detection with invalid inferences: All heuristics, no logic (2025) Memory and Cognition
finding: Two experiments (total N=248). Invalid syllogisms such as AC and DA are intuitively valid to many participants. Once believability and chosen response are controlled, valid and invalid items do not differ in reaction time or confidence. Reverse detection effects vanish if invalid items are treated as valid.
numbers: Total N=248 over two experiments.
limits: Abstract only. Weakens the claim that people always detect logic-heuristic conflict; conflict can be between two heuristics.
agent_relevance: A certainty signal can be flat even when the first answer is wrong, because the error feels right. Do not trust a single signal.

source: Taubenfeld et al. (2025) Confidence Improves Self-Consistency in LLMs (CISC)
finding: Weighting each sampled path by the model's own confidence cuts the number of samples needed. The best signal is the one that tells right from wrong answers to the SAME question, not the best-calibrated one.
numbers: Nine models, four datasets (MATH, GSM8K, BBH and one more). Average sample saving over 40%. Gemma2-9B on MATH: 8 CISC samples beat 30-sample self-consistency (73% cost reduction). Within-question discrimination (WQD) / CISC cost reduction at 10 samples: verbalised binary 52.2% / 10%; verbalised 0-100 56.1% / 30%; response probability 59.0% / 31%; P(True) 62.3% / 46%. ECE was best for verbalised binary (0.005) yet it was the weakest for CISC.
quote: the most calibrated confidence method proved to be the least effective for CISC
limits: Confidence is used as a vote weight, not as a trigger to rethink. Open-weight models, math and multiple-choice style tasks. P(True) and response probability need logits or a second call.
agent_relevance: Best signal in this study is P(True): ask the model whether its own answer is true. Judge signals by within-question ranking, not by calibration.

source: Kang, Zhao and Song (2025) Scalable Best-of-N Selection via Self-Certainty
finding: Self-certainty, the divergence of the token distribution from uniform, picks better answers from N samples than perplexity and scales with N like a reward model. It works on open-ended tasks where majority vote cannot.
numbers: Benchmarks: LiveBench-Math, GSM8K, MATH, CRUXEval-O, LiveCodeBench; Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct main model. Table text in the PDF was garbled, so per-cell numbers were not extracted. The text states self-certainty beats greedy, sampling and perplexity at equal N.
limits: Needs logits (white-box), so not usable for API-only agents without logprobs. Selection among samples, not a rethink trigger.
agent_relevance: Token-level certainty is a good ranker, but an API-only agent must fall back to agreement or P(True).

source: Li et al. (2024) Escape Sky-high Cost: Early-Stopping Self-Consistency (ESC), ICLR
finding: Sample in small windows and stop when a whole window gives one answer. The number of samples drops a lot with about the same accuracy.
numbers: Average samples saved: MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CommonsenseQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4%. Accuracy comparable.
limits: Stops sampling; it does not decide to rethink after a committed answer. Older models.
agent_relevance: Agreement among cheap samples is a usable stop signal. The hardest set (MATH) saves least, which is the right direction.

source: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang and Mausam (2023) Adaptive-Consistency, EMNLP
finding: A Dirichlet model of answer counts decides when the majority is safe, so easy questions use few samples.
numbers: 17 reasoning and code datasets, three LLMs. Sample budget cut by up to 7.9 times with an average accuracy drop under 0.1%.
limits: Same limit as ESC: a stop rule for sampling, not a rethink-or-not policy tested against an always-rethink baseline.
agent_relevance: Closest published thing to a certainty-gated policy for API-only agents. Gap 1 stays open for rethinking proper, but a stop-on-agreement rule is validated.

source: Singhi et al. (2025) When To Solve, When To Verify, COLM
finding: At equal compute, spending tokens on more solutions with majority vote beats spending them on generative verification, except at very large budgets.
numbers: GenRM first matches self-consistency only after about 8x the inference compute and needs about 128x more compute to gain 3.8% over it. Holds for Llama and Qwen, 7B and 70B, and QwQ-32B on math.
limits: Tests verifier-style checking, not a gated rethink. Math only.
agent_relevance: Equal-compute evidence against always-verify: unless the checker is cheap or external, extra samples win. A gate should save tokens by skipping checks on agreed answers.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration: Eliciting Calibrated Confidence from RLHF Language Models
finding: For RLHF chat models, a stated confidence is better calibrated than the token probability on factual QA.
numbers: TriviaQA, SciQ, TruthfulQA. Verbalised confidence often reduces expected calibration error by about 50% relative (ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude).
limits: Factual QA, not reasoning. Calibration (ECE) is not the same as ranking right against wrong (CISC shows the two can disagree). Older chat models.
agent_relevance: Verbalised confidence is cheap and API-friendly but only one of several signals; compare by ranking, not calibration.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? Survey, TACL
finding: Critical survey. No prior work shows reliable self-correction from prompting alone on general tasks. Self-correction works where reliable external feedback exists, or where the response is decomposable. Many positive papers use oracle information or weak baseline prompts.
numbers: Qualitative survey; no pooled effect size.
limits: A review of others' numbers. The crossover is stated as a condition (reliable external signal), not as a measured threshold.
agent_relevance: Put external checks (tests, tools) in the loop; allow same-model review only when the task has a decomposable check.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs can self-correct with tool-interactive critiquing, ICLR
finding: Tool feedback helps more than no-tool critique, but the gap is task-dependent: small on GSM8K, large on QA. The authors say models mostly do not know what they know, so self-verification can lower accuracy. Gains are largest under oracle gating.
numbers: Text-davinci-003 GSM8K: PoT 70.1; CRITIC with tool 72.2 (+2.1); CRITIC without tool 68.3 (-1.8); oracle (only incorrect answers corrected) 77.4. SVAMP: 80.7 with tool and 80.7 without (PoT 84.0). TabMWP: with tool 87.6 (+23.0), without tool 84.9 (+20.3), so the no-tool loop is not uniformly bad. AmbigNQ EM: CoT 44.2, CRITIC 50.0, without tool 42.0, oracle 59.8.
limits: Table layout in the PDF text was partly garbled; ChatGPT rows are not used. Oracle rows use ground truth on which answers to correct, which a real agent lacks. One older model.
agent_relevance: Quantifies the crossover: on math with a weak model, tools add about 2 to 4 points over no-tool; QA gain is 8 points. Oracle gating adds 5+ more, which is the prize for a good trigger.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Gains come from a feedback signal, here unit tests the model writes itself. When that signal has many false positives, reflection stops early and does not help.
numbers: GPT-4 pass@1 HumanEval Python 80 to 91; MBPP Python 80 to 77 (worse); HumanEval Rust 60 to 68; MBPP Rust 71 to 75. False-positive test rate (tests pass, solution wrong): 1.4% on HumanEval Python, 16.3% on MBPP Python.
limits: Tests are self-generated, so it is not pure external feedback. One model family. Authors name false positives as the failure cause.
agent_relevance: A trigger only helps if its false-positive rate is low: a wrong 'pass' stops the loop early. Measure the false-positive rate of any certainty gate.

source: Valmeekam, Marquez and Kambhampati (2023) Can LLMs Really Improve by Self-critiquing Their Own Plans?
finding: On Blocksworld planning with GPT-4, a sound external verifier gives much more gain than an LLM verifier, which accepts many bad plans.
numbers: 100 instances: no backprompting 40%; LLM verifier plus backprompting 55% (3.48 iterations); sound verifier (VAL) plus backprompting 88% (4.18 iterations). LLM verifier accuracy 61/100; it called 38 of 45 invalid plans valid (84.5% false positives); true positive rate 54/55 (98.2%).
limits: Part of the +15 for LLM critique may come from extra attempts, which the authors note. The abstract says self-critique diminishes performance, but the table shows a small gain over no backprompting; the big jump is the sound verifier. One domain, GPT-4.
agent_relevance: Crossover evidence: blind review accepts nearly all bad plans, so it stops too soon. A sound check adds 48 points over none.

source: Stechly, Marquez and Kambhampati (2023) GPT-4 Doesn't Know It's Wrong: Iterative Prompting for Reasoning Problems
finding: Graph colouring with GPT-4: self-critique makes things worse; a sound verifier helps, but the content of the feedback hardly matters. The gain is mostly from more tries.
numbers: Baseline 16% with no backprompt. With the LLM as its own verifier: 1 of 100 correct. With a sound verifier: near 40%; binary, single-error and full-error feedback were not different. Same 40% when the verifier only stops the loop and the LLM writes the critique.
limits: One task family, GPT-4 only. Authors argue the gain is resampling plus verifier selection, not reasoning from feedback.
agent_relevance: Supports a trigger based on an external accept test with resampling, rather than reflection. The check, not the critique text, carries the value.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling (budget forcing with Wait)
finding: Appending 'Wait' when the model tries to stop makes a fine-tuned reasoning model keep checking and raises AIME24 score, but only up to about six forced continuations.
numbers: s1-32B AIME24: 50.0 with no forcing; 53.3 with Wait 1x and 2x; 56.7 with Wait 4x (30 problems, so one problem = 3.3 points). MATH500 92.6 to 93.0 (2x); GPQA 56.6 to 59.6. On AIME24, 'Wait' (53.3) beat 'Hmm' and 'Alternatively' (both 50.0 at 2x). Gains flatten at 6x; too many suppressions cause loops.
limits: Not equal tokens: forcing adds tokens. AIME24 has 30 items, so gains are 1 to 2 problems. Model trained on 1,000 traces; effect not shown for other models.
agent_relevance: A forced second look helps on hard problems for that model. At equal token cost the picture is mixed (see d17, d18).

source: Ghosal et al. (2025) Does Thinking More Always Help? Mirage of Test-Time Scaling
finding: Extending thinking by appending 'Wait' helps at first, then accuracy falls. The authors link the early rise to higher output variance, not better reasoning. At the same token budget, parallel samples with majority vote do better.
numbers: Three models (R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and 7B, R1-Distill-Llama-8B), GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME24. R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on GSM8K: raising budget from 385 to 16,000 tokens by Wait cost 11.8% accuracy; parallel thinking at the same budget gained 10.1%. At 16K tokens parallel thinking was about 22% above Wait-and-think-more and 47% above exact-length thinking; abstract says up to 20% over extended thinking.
limits: Small distilled models. Wait was repeated until an exact token count, a stress test and not how a gated agent would use it.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 5 for reasoning models: blind 'Wait' at equal tokens loses to resampling. Rethink only when a signal says so.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Wait, We Don't Need to 'Wait'! Removing Thinking Tokens (NoWait)
finding: Suppressing 'Wait' and 'Hmm' tokens during decoding shortens the chain without losing accuracy in R1-style models.
numbers: Ten benchmarks (text, image, video), five R1-style model series. Chain length cut by 27% to 51% with no loss in utility, per the abstract.
limits: Abstract-level numbers; per-model tables not extracted. Pure efficiency claim; some tasks may need reflection.
agent_relevance: Counterweight to d16: much of the reflection text is not needed. Reflection tokens are worth gating.

source: Su et al. (2025) Between Underthinking and Overthinking: Reasoning Length and Correctness
finding: For a fixed question, accuracy rises with response length and then falls. Wrong answers are longer than right ones. Models spend extra tokens on easy problems and too few on problems beyond them, so they misjudge difficulty.
numbers: Two models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B and DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview), GSM8K and MATH, N=10 samples per question for difficulty tiers (Easy = 10 of 10 right, Hard = 0 of 10). On MATH, wrong answers averaged over 6,000 tokens and right ones under 3,000. Preference tuning for shorter answers with no labels cut 10-25% off correct response length.
limits: Two small models, math only. Length is a correlate; hard questions are longer for both reasons.
agent_relevance: Response length is a free, black-box warning signal: a long answer is more likely wrong. Cheap input for a trigger.

source: Hassid et al. (2025) Don't Overthink it: Preferring Shorter Thinking Chains
finding: Within a question, the shortest of several sampled chains is the most accurate. Stopping after the first few finished chains saves tokens.
numbers: Shortest chain is up to 34.5% more accurate than the longest and up to 18.8% above a random pick, and 50% to 67% shorter. short-1@k matches majority vote using up to 40% fewer thinking tokens; short-3@k beats majority voting at all budgets with up to 33% less wall time.
limits: Math and reasoning benchmarks with open reasoning models; length selection needs parallel samples.
agent_relevance: Length rank among parallel samples is a cheap, API-compatible signal that needs no logits.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu and Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally
finding: Best way to spend compute depends on question difficulty. Easy questions favour sequential revisions; hard ones favour parallel search. Difficulty is binned into five levels from the base model's own pass rate.
numbers: Compute-optimal allocation beats best-of-N using about 4x less compute for both revisions and search (MATH, PaLM 2-S*). In a FLOPs-matched view, a smaller model with test-time compute beats a 14x larger one on easy and intermediate questions, but not reliably on the hardest.
limits: The model-predicted difficulty bin uses 2048 samples per question and a learned verifier; the paper says this cost is not charged to the savings and leaves it open. Math only.
agent_relevance: Difficulty before solving helps in principle, but the published estimate is not cheap. A first short pass may serve as the difficulty probe.

source: Cuadron et al. (2025) The Danger of Overthinking: Reasoning-Action Dilemma in Agentic Tasks
finding: On SWE-bench Verified, higher overthinking scores (thinking instead of acting on environment feedback) go with fewer resolved issues. Reasoning models score about three times higher on overthinking than non-reasoning models.
numbers: 4,018 trajectories scored by an LLM judge that correlates with human experts. o1 high effort: 29.1% resolved at $1,400; o1 low effort: 21.0% at $400. Choosing the lowest overthinking score of k=2 low-effort runs: 27.3% at 43% lower cost than high effort; k=3: 30.3% using 15% less compute.
limits: One benchmark (software engineering), one model family, judge-based score. The 'almost 30%' headline is a relative gain. Scoring happens after the trajectory, so it selects; it is not a live stop signal.
agent_relevance: The pattern transfers to agentic work, but the mitigation shown was post-hoc selection and native function calling, so a live stop signal is not shown.

source: Liu and Wang (2025) Answer Convergence as a Signal for Early Stopping in Reasoning
finding: Models usually reach their final answer after about 60% of the reasoning steps on math. Stopping when the answer stops changing, or learning when to stop from hidden states, saves tokens.
numbers: Five benchmarks, five open-weight LLMs. Answer-consistency early stop cut tokens by over 40% on NaturalQuestions with a small accuracy gain; the learned stop reduced tokens by 46.2% in one setting.
limits: Overlaps with the earlier probe work (a21). Needs intermediate answer probes (extra tokens or hidden states).
agent_relevance: Matches Chen's overthinking finding: the first answer is usually right; a stable answer is a stop signal.

source: Wu et al. (2025) Thought calibration: Efficient and confident test-time scaling
finding: Linear probes on hidden states decide when thinking has plateaued, with a statistical guarantee on risk from conformal calibration.
numbers: Three reasoning models, four datasets. Up to 60% fewer thinking tokens on in-distribution data and up to 20% fewer out of distribution, with performance kept. The supervised probe stayed over-confident out of distribution.
limits: Needs hidden states (white-box). The guarantee holds only when test data match the calibration set.
agent_relevance: A calibrated risk budget can set the stop threshold; the drop from 60% to 20% out of distribution warns against moving thresholds across tasks.

source: Fu et al. (2024) Efficiently Scaling LLM Reasoning with Certaindex (Dynasor)
finding: Certaindex measures how stable intermediate answers are. Used as a gate, it lets easy requests stop early and gives hard ones more tokens, on a serving system.
numbers: Up to 50% compute saved at the same accuracy in batch inference; up to 3.3x more queries or 4.7x tighter latency targets in online serving. Reasoning models used about 3x more tokens than needed in one test.
limits: Systems paper; accuracy-versus-allocation curves by difficulty are not the main result. Numbers from the abstract and intro.
agent_relevance: Closest certainty-gated allocation result, dynamic across items; relevant to gap 1 and gap 6.
